title: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says
description: The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.Lo
body: The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.Lord Ricketts said more money should be spent on the defence budget, as well as improving the resilience of energy, transport and air traffic control.He warned hybrid attacks were becoming "more reckless, more dangerous" and that people could end up being killed. It comes after MI5 chief Sir Kevin McCallum said in his annual speech earlier this week that threats from foreign states, including Russia and Iran, had quadrupled in the last decade.Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ministers had to warn British people about what might be coming."Not only is [Russian President Vladimir] Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he's also trying to undermine morale in European countries," he said.He said there had been a stark warning from the head of MI5 that there could be worse to come in terms of hybrid attacks in the UK or on other Nato territory.Responding to a question about the impact of disruption by Russia, Lord Ricketts said: "I'm not saying there's going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain."But yes these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous...people are going to end up getting killed somewhere." Hybrid attacks tend to use non-military methods, such as hacking, in an attempt to destabilise a country. Moscow is suspected to be behind many such attacks in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, but it has always denied involvement.As well as cyber-attacks, hybrid attacks can include attempts at sabotage and efforts to spread misinformation. Lord Ricketts's warning comes after US President Donald Trump blocked sanctions on Russia. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the decision "only encourages him [Putin] to keep attacking" Ukraine. The former national security adviser, who also previously ran the Foreign Office, said the UK's focus should be on putting more effort into the coalition of the willing, rather than attempting to act as a bridge between Zelensky and Trump."I don't think in Trump's current mood there is any influence Britain can have in the short term," he said.A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.Last month, Germany said Russia was responsible for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig, in which an explosive failed to detonate close to Ukrainian cargo planes.French President Emmanuel Macron warned in September that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France had intensified.

schema.headline: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says

title: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says
description: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replac
body: The long-running home renovation TV series DIY SOS will be "rested" next year in the light of "savings challenges", the BBC has said.It will be replaced by a spin-off show featuring highlights from past episodes. Sources denied reports in the Sun newspaper the programme would be axed as part of a plan to make savings. Presented by Nick Knowles, DIY SOS sees a team transform the homes of families who are facing severe illness, disability, bereavement or building disasters.It was first broadcast in 1999 and is currently airing its 35th series on BBC One and iPlayer.The decision comes during the corporation's drive to save £500m over three years. It has already cancelled several well-known TV shows including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind and Live At The Apollo.A BBC spokesperson said: "In light of the BBC's savings challenges we have taken the decision to rest DIY SOS in 2027 and commission a new spin-off show instead from producers South Shore."DIY SOS Rebuilt My Life will revisit successes from the show's past and expand the brand on the BBC in a more cost-effective way next year."

schema.headline: DIY SOS to be 'rested' next year to save money, BBC says

title: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal
description: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scanda
body: It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers. Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

schema.headline: Trial of German steakhouse heiress Christina Block that sparked a huge spy scandal

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
description: Image source, ReutersByMax MatzaUpdated 2 hours agoDonald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect,
body: Image source, ReutersByMax MatzaUpdated 2 hours agoDonald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by Trump in September.But the US president issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US "national interest", prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine then accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy, giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer have criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X. The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.Figure caption, Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise?He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.He also said negotiators Ukrainian spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week.Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.Trump has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Middle East conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring ahead of the US midterm elections. Rising inflation has soured Trump's standing with the American public.Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel. Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days which saw several fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.This prompted scathing condemnation from Trump, who called the strikes a "disgrace". Zelensky replied that he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests". Image source, ReutersImage caption, Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnightConcerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.  Last week Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks. During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing and deliberately slowing down Ukraine's Starlink network.Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours.They said an ambulance driver was killed and 20 others were injured in Russian strikes on the city of Kherson on Saturday morning.Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.Additional reporting by Helen Sullivan

schema.headline: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies

title: Vaping: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked
description: When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking."I literally used to tell peo
body: When vaping first took off at Gracey Mungulu's school, she was vocal about the fact she found it as repulsive as smoking."I literally used to tell people like, 'Er, why are you doing that?'" she says.But Gracey says the habit became so common among her classmates that by the age of 16 she too had taken it up, even though the first time left her coughing rather than inhaling."The more you see it, the more you start trying it a bit more," Gracey says, "and then eventually I just got used to it and I was just doing it all the time."Now 21, she buys a refillable vape every day, using it whenever her hands aren't busy with her work as a hairdresser and in a school.Gracey is among the more than one million people in the UK who say they have never smoked but now vape, according to recent Office for National Statistics (ONS) survey data – and that number has risen year-on-year.When vaping first came to the market it was seen as a way to help smokers quit cigarettes.Vaping nicotine, a highly addictive substance, is less harmful than cigarettes, but the long-term effects are not yet clear, according to the NHS.So why are people like Gracey, who have never smoked a cigarette, taking it up?The Londoner believes vaping helps when she's feeling socially anxious."It's the hand action," she says, "just having something in your hand, just having something in your mouth."Like cigarettes Gracey's vape contains nicotine, a highly addictive substance that triggers withdrawal symptoms like irritability and anxiety when it leaves your system.Vaping has become a "mindless action," she says. When she answers the call to talk to BBC News for this article, Gracey says that without thinking about it, she had been lying in bed, with her vape in one hand, and her other hand scrolling Instagram.The habitual aspect of regular vaping is something GP Dr Helen Wall hears a lot from her patients."It's that kind of psychological dependence on something else to almost regulate their emotions," she says.Like Gracey, Malin Andersson, who vaped until recently, says her habit went hand in hand with doomscrolling. She had also tried cigarettes but never considered herself a smoker.At 33, she falls in the age range most likely to vape. The ONS report suggests nearly one in six people aged 25-34 in the UK may use e-cigarettes daily or occasionally.The domestic abuse campaigner and former Love Island contestant started vaping when she was going through a stressful break-up and looking for comfort. She believes it was the physical action that got her hooked."It's a dopamine hit," Malin says. "It's literally an adult's version of a dummy."She says it was dulling her senses and leaving her demotivated.Malin became so frustrated with how reliant she had become on her banana ice-flavoured vape that she quit in May this year."It was annoying me so much that it was always in my hand that I'd end up throwing it across the room," she says. Alex, from Manchester, also gradually formed a vaping habit, which started after she occasionally vaped on nights out and then began to take the vapes home.The 26-year-old, who didn't want to give her last name, says the habit would become such a constant part of her life that she would work while "lying in my bed with my laptop in front of me and then my vape on my chest".Prof Sarah Jackson, from the University College London Alcohol and Tobacco Research Group, points out that while "alarm bells" may ring at the recent ONS figures, it could be the case that some of the people in this group would have started smoking if they hadn't started vaping."In which case, vaping has diverted them away from a more harmful behaviour, which is good news," she says. "On the other hand, there will be people that are being exposed to more risk than they would have otherwise."She points to a 2024 study from UCL researchers that found nicotine use had risen among young adults in England, although cigarette smoking had declined. "We can infer from that that some of the people who are vaping wouldn't have smoked otherwise," Jackson says.The ONS report says about 5.4 million people aged 16 and over vape in Britain, while the number of smokers of all ages continues to steadily fall. Some 4.9 million adults in the UK  smoke.The UK is aiming to cut smoking rates and reduce the appeal of vaping among children and young people.The marketing of vapes - which has featured bright colours and sweet flavours - is being looked at, with a recent government consultation on new measures expected to give a response in due course.Within the 1.1 million vapers who never smoked, "there probably is a group who would not be vaping [without] the marketing of vaping which is very prominent", says Hazel Cheeseman from charity Action on Smoking and Health.The NHS warns non-smokers and those aged 17 and under to never vape, while it's illegal for anyone under 18 to buy vapes. Disposable vapes - seen as a key driver in the rise of youth vaping – were banned last year.Wall says the heavy marketing of vapes in recent years has helped to fuel a "misconception" that they are "safe and not addictive".Gracey thinks vapes should be sold in the same standardised plain packaging as cigarettes because it "looks scary"."With vapes, they have all these flavours, all these pretty colours - it's just making us more attracted to it".While she says vaping is seen as far more socially acceptable among her generation than smoking, she finds her habit problematic and has considered quitting to save the £35 a week it costs her.But just like smoking, giving up vaping can be a struggle. And for Alex, vaping led her in the opposite direction.She says she managed to quit vaping while travelling for several months, but with no access to vapes she began smoking cigarettes for the first time instead.Cigarettes are not considered a healthy or helpful way to stop vaping by experts. The NHS strongly advises people to stop smoking, and it remains the leading cause of preventable illness and premature death in the UK.To quit vaping the NHS suggests gradually reducing the strength of the vape's nicotine, increasing the time between vaping sessions, or switching to a suitable nicotine replacement therapy product. But professional support to stop vaping is patchy, with a recent survey, external finding fewer than half (45%) of healthcare providers in England offered vaping cessation support. There is a mixed picture of support to quit across the rest of the UK. While it is good fewer people are smoking, Wall says that for people like Gracey who go straight to vapes a bit of the messaging has been missed.  "Vaping was only intended [by the NHS] to be a replacement for cigarettes."

schema.headline: Vaping: Why people who have never smoked are getting hooked

title: Halloween costumes 2026: From Obsession to Odyssey, the top TV, film and pop culture party outfits
description: The whimsical fashion trend, which has dominated social media feeds in 2026, is also predicted to be a big influence this Halloween for women. Think g
body: The whimsical fashion trend, which has dominated social media feeds in 2026, is also predicted to be a big influence this Halloween for women. Think gargoyles, moths, mushrooms, woodland fairies and 17th Century Pierrot clowns.In keeping with the theme, Lauren Sidebottom, a TikTok beauty and fashion creator from Leeds, is planning on dressing up as a weeping angel.The 23-year-old, who studied theatrical makeup at college, says she'll be creating the look using body paint, grey tights, a cracking makeup effect on her skin, drawn-on tears, and a grey wig.Women her age are, she says "wanting to look cool, different, not like every other girl," with their whimsical costumes.Tiggy Bellinger, 21, from West Sussex, agrees DIY costumes can help avoid people wearing "the exact same thing".

title: Harry Styles debuts emotional new song dedicated to Liam Payne
description: Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne. The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, c
body: Harry Styles performed an unreleased song he wrote for his former One Direction bandmate Liam Payne. The Grammy Award-winning star played the track, called What Is Enough, during his sold-out concert at Madison Square Garden, on the second anniversary of Payne's death. Styles is currently performing at the New York venue as part of a residency on his record-breaking Together, Together tour. Addressing the packed crowd on Friday night, the singer paid tribute to Payne as a friend and someone he "wouldn't have been able to do this without".As a spotlight shone over him, Styles made a moving speech, in which he honoured Liam Payne, who died two years ago after falling from a hotel balcony in Argentina."I feel incredibly lucky to get to play these shows here in New York, and this building means a lot to me," said the artist. "There are so many people in my life, friends and people that I've worked with that I wouldn't have been able to do this without," he continued."And two years ago today, I lost one of those friends."This was met with cheers from the audience, who were hearing What Is Enough for the first time. Wearing a royal blue jumper with a red collar, the musician then urged fans to keep an eye out for and support each other. "I'm sure a lot of you have been through similar things. I hope you haven't. "But really, it's just about looking after each other."He added that there were "so many more people who have touched my life in such special ways", thanking those who helped him get to where he is. "I'm gonna play you a song I wrote for my friend about two years ago, if that's all right."As he paused, passionate cheers and clapping could be heard from his fans.The singer then began to play his guitar and perform What is Enough, which featured emotional and reflective lyrics.As he sang out to the crowd, his band played a melodic accompaniment.Sharing their reaction to Friday night's performance on Instagram,, external Harry Styles' fans described What is Enough as "beautiful".Styles launched his solo career in 2017 after becoming a global star in One Direction.His first album and single were both UK number ones, while his record Harry's House won a Grammy and a Brit Award after its release in 2022. Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Harry Styles debuts emotional new song dedicated to Liam Payne

title: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery
description: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-yea
body: Pope Leo XIV has been discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital, just four days after an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung.The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, stopping to speak to well-wishers.The Vatican said the Pope will give the traditional Angelus prayer and blessing to a crowd in St Peter's Square on Sunday, as he did last week when he surprised the world by announcing the surgery.On Friday, photographs were released of the Pope celebrating Mass and distributing communion in hospital for staff. A statement from his doctors said blood tests and a chest X-ray showed "steady improvement" following his operation.The surgery on Tuesday, which lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. The results of further tests to check for any sign that the cancer has spread have not yet been announced.The Pope also spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, in their first call since June 2025. The Vatican said the call was to urge "dialogue and peace".It came as Russia's bombardment of cities across Ukraine intensifies, with a growing number of civilian casualties and no sign of Putin being ready to halt the invasion.The Pope also called for a humanitarian ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshkiy, occupied by Russia and under constant shelling, to allow people to be evacuated and for the urgent delivery of food and medicine. The BBC recently reported on residents there being forced to eat garden weeds to survive.The Pope's schedule has been cleared completely until 20 October, so his reappearance in public so soon is a surprise and will be some relief for Catholics around the world.Those close to the Pope said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America, planned for early November and which includes a visit to Peru, where he was a missionary for many years.It is not yet clear whether he might be fit to travel or require further treatment.

schema.headline: Pope discharged from hospital days after lung cancer surgery

title: Boy and man die in light air craft crash near Loch Lomond
description: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch LomondImage caption, The light aircraft crashed a few miles north east of Drymen ne
body: Boy, 16, and 80-year-old man die in light aircraft crash near Loch LomondImage caption, The light aircraft crashed a few miles north east of Drymen near StirlingByClaire DiamondBBC ScotlandUpdated 2 hours agoA 16-year-old boy and an 80-year-old man have died following a light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond in Scotland. Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash near the village of Drymen, in the Stirling Council area, at about 16:45 BST on Friday. The boy and man were pronounced dead and their next of kin have been informed, police said.Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) conducts its inquiries. An AAIB spokesperson said: "A team has travelled to the accident site near Drymen, north of Glasgow, to make inquiries and gather evidence as part of the process of conducting a safety investigation."Image caption, Police remained at the scene on Saturday morningOfficers were at the scene, near Old Drymen Road, on Saturday, and have cordoned off a gate leading to a hill where the crash appears to have happened.A police van and a team of officers were seen travelling up to the site on Saturday morning.The Piper Tomahawk II aircraft is registered to Leading Edge Flight Training in Renfrew, according to the Civil Aviation Authority's aircraft register, external. It took off from Glasgow Airport on Friday afternoon at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of Drymen. Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The light aircraft took off from Glasgow Airport, before crashing near Drymen The plane had earlier taken off from Cumbernauld Airport at 11:46, before flying 15 minutes to Glasgow Airport. It stayed there until about 13:00, before doing a two-hour flight north east to Newport on Tay then turning round and heading back to Glasgow.It was on the ground at the airport for just over an hour before it took off again and started its final flight.  Gavin Birch-Williams, managing director of Glasgow Airport, said: "We are aware of an incident involving a light aircraft that departed from Glasgow Airport."This is a deeply tragic event, and the thoughts and heartfelt sympathies from all at Glasgow Airport are with the friends and families affected."Drymen resident Colin Cameron told BBC Scotland News he knew there was a major incident because of all the emergency service activity. He said he had seen police, ambulances, a serious incident unit and specialist fire engines, as well as two helicopters. It was not until Saturday morning that he heard it had been a light air craft crash, which he described as "awful".

schema.headline: Boy and man die in light air craft crash near Loch Lomond

title: England rugby league: 'Positives' from Tonga shock - but is their World Cup over?
description: As Tonga's deliriously happy supporters celebrated in their thousands in Perth, England knew they only had themselves to blame.They had passed up plen
body: As Tonga's deliriously happy supporters celebrated in their thousands in Perth, England knew they only had themselves to blame.They had passed up plenty of chances to win their 2026 Rugby League World Cup opener and had arguably been the better side for the opening 20 minutes of both halves.But a succession of mistakes - handling errors, needless offloads, sloppy penalties – allowed Tonga to control the momentum for much of the game.By the time Haumole Olakau'atu crashed over for Tonga's fourth try in their 30-12 victory, it was all over. The question is whether England's World Cup hopes are also over already.Not so, insists coach Brian McDermott."It was a really good contest, when it wasn't it was down to us and the errors we made," he told his post-match media conference."We stood toe to toe for nearly all the game, but we made errors chasing the scoreboard. I'm not going to say it's an easy fix, but it's something I can change."We know what is in front of us now. We have to win the next two games. I have seen enough to say we are heading in the right direction."We were not strategically outdone. There are tonnes of positives to take out of tonight, but one or two things we must get rid of, like losing possession."Due to the vagaries of the international rugby league calendar, this was McDermott's first match in charge of England since being appointed in April as Shaun Wane's successor.Wane had his critics, many of them justified, but he organised a defensively solid England team who whitewashed Tonga on their tour of Britain in 2023.He left in January after England were well beaten in last year's Ashes, and McDermott has had to piece together a team with minimal preparation.England did not play a single warm-up match; this was their first game since losing to Australia at Headingley in November 2025. They have not won a match since November 2024, against Samoa.A much more assured Tonga side started the evening with a spine-tingling Sipi Tau battle dance and ended it with victory for the first time in seven meetings with England.The relative lack of preparation is out of McDermott's control. Team selection and tactics are not, and that is where the former Leeds Rhinos coach will be questioned."You cannot play with freedom at international level, you have to keep hold of the ball," McDermott said after the game. His side looked nervous with ball in hand, too willing to pass up the chance to run at the Tongans and pass the buck.As for selection, McDermott chose a central pairing of Harry Smith and captain George Williams. They were found wanting, with Williams enduring one of his poorest games in an England shirt.AJ Brimson was chosen ahead of Jack Welsby at full-back. Although Brimson scored England's first try, he was also caught out of position for Tonga's fourth.McDermott said he will "have a look" at options regarding selection. Expect changes when the team to face France is named on Tuesday."You have to give Tonga credit for the scramble, but I reckon we left three or four [opportunities] out there early doors," said Williams. "We lost our way, we were erratic, we must find that balance to improve the team."We can't be kicking stones. We have a great group of lads, and one loss does not change how we think."But will one loss cost England a place in the semi-finals? The complicated group phase makes that possible.There are six nations in the combined Group B-C, but all the teams play just three opponents - think a scaled down version of the league phase in football's Champions League. The top two in the overall table reach the semis.If sides are level on points, head-to-head is the first tiebreaker that will be considered, rather than points difference. But because not everyone in the group plays each other, it may yet be that points difference becomes crucial. England must win their next two games, against France next Saturday and Papua New Guinea on 30 October, to stand a realistic chance of progression.If they do, results elsewhere then become a factor - and it could get complicated.And there is the strong possibility that England will not know their fate for certain until two days later, when Tonga face 2022 finalists Samoa in their last group game.England's best bet, it seems, is to rack up huge wins in the next two games and hope for the best."We want to rack up some points," England wing Dom Young said. "You know, we're good enough to do it."Maybe England are good enough – but not if they keep making the same mistakes again and again.

schema.headline: England rugby league: 'Positives' from Tonga shock - but is their World Cup over?

title: Two-week half terms - the school holiday no-one can agree on
description: Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school
body: Samantha Buckland is bracing herself for a tough fortnight. The single mum lives in Reigate, Surrey, and her seven-year-old son goes to a state school that has just introduced a two-week half term.Buckland has two jobs: teaching medical students at a hospital in Brighton and working at a vintage shop in her home town. The 45-year-old receives universal credit and is worried about the cost of looking after her son while school is closed."What I'm trying to do is find out who I can get childcare from and work around that," she says. "I'd like to work, I need money. It's not cheap to live these days."But money isn't Buckland's only concern. She's also trying to piece together the patchwork of childcare needed to cover the break.There's a local holiday club, but it's only running for one of the two weeks, which Buckland says "parents are up in arms about". She'll also have to work at the hospital some days.As a result, she's considering asking family to help, or even going to stay with a fellow mum so they can take turns with the kids.The number of pupils in England attending academies has grown rapidly in the past decade, according to Department for Education data, external published in June 2026. Indeed, 60.4% of all pupils now attend an academy.As academies spread, the school calendar is becoming increasingly fragmented - creating fresh challenges for parents.Alistair Pringle, 42, lives in Washington in Tyne and Wear with his wife, a teacher, and two children aged 11 and six. His eldest has just started at a secondary academy with a two-week half term, while his youngest goes to a primary academy with a one-week half term."This is the first time we've had to deal with different half terms," Pringle says. His children and wife will be off together for the first week. His eldest then has a second week off, but by then the others will have returned to class.Pringle works full-time in marketing - often in the office - but is fortunate his employer "can accommodate it if I need to work from home"."The thing that concerns me is not so much the childcare, it's the fact that I have to work," he says. "Yes, my eldest would be at home and she'd be looked after, but what's she getting out of that second week?"Lucy Walker-Etchells, 40, is a teacher at Dixons Brooklands Academy in south Manchester. Her school has a two-week half term, but for the majority of her teaching career she's had one week."I definitely much prefer two weeks," Walker-Etchells says. "Most teachers would agree because autumn is an intense term. It's really nice to have two weeks to recharge and come back feeling refreshed."Moving a week's holiday from the summer to the autumn half term could benefit pupils too, she believes."Sometimes, vulnerable students really struggle being off for so long over the six-week holiday if they're in difficult circumstances," she says. "That's a long time out of structure, so I don't think it's a bad thing to break up the summer holidays."Unity Schools Partnership runs 40 primary, secondary and special schools across the east of England. The trust introduced a two-week half term in autumn 2023 and asked parents and staff how they felt about the switch the following year.Their consultation found 58% of parents were in favour of the two-week break, with the remainder against. Strikingly, 89% of staff supported it."It's cited as a reason why they would stay with us as an employer, which helps us build quality in schools," says Dominic Norrish, Unity's chief executive.He adds that the number of days lost to staff sickness absence has fallen by 16% since the two-week half term was brought in. "People are getting ill less frequently because they've got longer to recover between half terms," he reflects.Ultimately, getting the best teachers in front of pupils more regularly means "children will receive a better education in the autumn term".

schema.headline: Two-week half terms - the school holiday no-one can agree on

title: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year
description: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a prof
body: Eknoor Singh says he only needs his mobile phone and a decent internet connection to earn more than £120,000 a year.The 22-year-old Londoner is a professional "clipper". He is paid by clients to make short, vertical videos for social media, in the hope of them going viral."The more views a clip gets, the more money I make," he says.The way it typically works is that the client - who could be anyone from a clothing brand to a record label, movie studio, podcaster or influencer - has a longer video that the clipper watches first.He or she then makes 30 to 60-second clips of what they consider to be the best bit or bits, and uploads them to Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or other platforms.The idea is that the clippers, who are typically aged from 16 to 25, will have a better understanding of what will connect with that demographic, and get the short videos as many views as possible.For 24-year-old clipper Ethan Weems from Wichita, Kansas, it's a lucrative side hustle to his other video-making work. He says he makes "at least $1,000 a month" from clipping.He does this by making short videos for YouTuber and podcaster Caleb Hammer, who is best known for hosting a show called Financial Audit, which analyses the personal finances of his guests.Weems says clipping helps him make a living from home – giving him more time to spend with his wife and one-year-old son. "I don't want that typical nine-to-five job where I have to go into an office every day," he says.Yet while some clippers can make good money, social media consultant Lia Haberman cautions that there are very few of them. "It mirrors the creator economy more broadly. The vast majority make little to nothing," she says.Meanwhile, streaming industry analyst Devin Nash says it's easy to underestimate the time required to make clipping a success. He warns that successful clippers must "watch hours and hours of content, and they just live in that world".Connecting clippers with their prospective clients are a number of intermediary websites, where available video jobs are listed. These range from pages on general online forums such as Reddit and Discord, to dedicated clipping sites such as Clipping Culture, Vyro, Whop and Kick.The latter websites take a fee from the companies wanting the work done. Clipping Culture lists clients including Capital Records, Universal Music Group and HBO Max.For firms such as these, hiring a teenager or 20-something working from his or her bedroom is far cheaper than paying for traditional adverts on social media, and likely to be more effective in terms of getting eyeballs.That's the experience of Boxabl, a Las Vegas-based firm that makes modular homes. "I think we've done probably a billion views [of clips] so far," says founder Galiano Tiramani, who features in many of the company's videos.In the UK, Jimmy McLoughlin, a former Downing Street adviser and now host of the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast, has also embraced clips."The clips are almost like trailers for the main events," he says. For instance, a recent podcast with Prime Minister Andy Burnham "had close to 50,000 long plays, but in terms of clips, it's done millions".

schema.headline: The Sabrina Carpenter clip that helped a 22-year-old make £120,000 a year

title: Bournemouth recovery driver sentenced after runaway car crush
description: A vehicle recovery driver has been sentenced after he failed to secure a Range Rover that later rolled down a hill, dragging him along and crushing a
body: A vehicle recovery driver has been sentenced after he failed to secure a Range Rover that later rolled down a hill, dragging him along and crushing a member of the public who tried to help.Sean Baker, a driver for GRS Recovery Bournemouth, was sentenced to 14 weeks in prison, suspended for one year, at Bournemouth Crown Court on Friday.CCTV showed the two-tonne vehicle rolling down Exeter Crescent during a recovery operation on 22 March 2024, with Baker caught by a rear wheel.Kai Dransfield was on a break from his job at TGI Fridays when he saw Baker trapped under the runaway car "hanging on for dear life" and tried to help, only to be struck by the 4x4.Dransfield said: "He made eye contact with me, and my first thought was to just grab him to try and help him."But in his attempt to help, Dransfield was hit by the vehicle and pulled underneath it.The vehicle rolled over both of his legs, causing serious injuries including multiple broken bones in his legs and fractures to his spine, according to the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).Dransfield continues to suffer chronic pain more than two years after the incident, and has difficulty walking.An HSE investigation found Baker had initially attached a winch to the front of the Range Rover, which would have prevented the vehicle rolling away if the handbrake was released or failed.But Baker later removed the winch, jacked up the vehicle and placed skates beneath the rear wheels, it said.Because the wheels were not secured with chocks, and no breakaway cables were attached, there was nothing preventing the vehicle from rolling backwards when it was lowered on to the skates.The investigation concluded Baker failed to take reasonable care for his own safety and that of others by not following established recovery procedures.The HSE also found his actions fell below the standard expected of a competent and experienced recovery driver.Baker later pleaded guilty to breaching Section 7 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.Speaking after the sentencing hearing, HSE inspector Alexander Ashen said: "Sean Baker was an experienced recovery driver."Failing to properly secure a vehicle weighing more than two tonnes on a steep hill was a fundamental error."This happened in a busy town centre, close to restaurants and car parks, with vehicles, motorcyclists and pedestrians regularly passing through the area."Sean Baker's failings were substantial, they exposed everyone nearby to risk and resulted in a member of the public, who stepped in to help, suffering life-changing injuries."Additional reporting by the Press Association

schema.headline: Bournemouth recovery driver sentenced after runaway car crush

title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
description: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feed
body: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switchFigure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they workByTiffanie TurnbullSydneyWarning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorderVarsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day."I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC."I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBCImage caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorderIt is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.The choiceFlynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order."You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC."I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC NewsImage caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social mediaNowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction, external; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health, external, and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline.Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line."The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.Image source, Cordelia Hsu/ReutersImage caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change."Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off."This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said."If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesImage caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) announcing the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m)."The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.The challengesThere's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise."I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoymentRight-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media banThe EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that."Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation, external.On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act.Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesImage caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feedsThe rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app.Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global."We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing."Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them.Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment."Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms – though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off.Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice."On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good."If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off?
